One of them, their own prophet, said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies. This testimony is true: for which cause rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not attending to Jewish fables and the commandments of men who turn themselves away from the truth. As far as the sequence of the discourse and the context of the passage are concerned, what he says, One of them, their own prophet, said, seems to be referred to those of whom he spoke above: "especially those who are of the circumcision, who must be restrained, who overturn whole houses, teaching what they ought not, for the sake of shameful gain", so that there follows: one of them, their own prophet, said. But because this little hexameter verse is found in none of the prophets who prophesied in Judea, it seems to me that it should be read in two ways: so that what he says, One of them, their own prophet, said, is joined with the earlier words, "for this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct the things that were lacking", and there follows: one of them, their own Prophet, said, that is, of the Cretans. But because much lies in between, and this seems absurd, and perhaps no one would accept it, it must therefore be fitted otherwise to the earlier words, which are nearer, so that we read: "For there are many who are also not submissive, empty talkers and deceivers of minds, but especially those who are of the circumcision"; these many, both not submissive, empty talkers and deceivers of minds, together with those who are of the circumcision, must be restrained, who overturn whole houses, teaching what they ought not, for the sake of shameful gain: one of them, their own Prophet, said; so that what he says, their own Prophet, is referred not specially to the Jews, and to those especially who are of the circumcision, but to the many who are not submissive, and empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, who, since they were certainly in Crete, must be believed to have been Cretans. Now this little verse is said to be found in the Oracles of Epimenides, the Cretan poet; whom he here called a prophet either mocking, namely that such Christians deserve to have such prophets, just as there were also prophets of Baal, and prophets of confusion, and others of stumblings, and whatever corrupt prophets Scripture mentions; or truly, because he wrote about Oracles and responses, which themselves foretell the future and proclaim long beforehand the things that are to come. Indeed the book itself is headed with the title Oracles; and because it seemed to promise something divine, I think the Apostle looked into it on that account, to see what the divination of the Gentiles promised, and at the right time made use of the little verse, writing to Titus, who was in Crete, so as to convict the false teachers of the Cretans by the island's own teacher. And Paul is found to have done this not only in this passage, but in others as well. For in the Acts of the Apostles, when he was addressing the people and disputing in the Areopagus, which is the senate house of the Athenians, he says among other things: "As certain of your own poets also have said: For we are also his offspring" (Acts 17), a half-line which is read in the Phaenomena of Aratus, whom Cicero translated into the Latin tongue, and Germanicus Caesar, and lately Avienus, and many whom it would take very long to enumerate. To the Corinthians too (1 Cor. 15:33), who were themselves polished with Attic eloquence and, because of the nearness of the places, seasoned with the savor of the Athenians, he took an iambic verse from a comedy of Menander: Evil conversations corrupt good morals. Nor is it any wonder if, as the occasion offered, he made use of the verses of Gentile poets, since, changing some things in the inscription of an altar, he even spoke to the Athenians: "For passing through," he says, "and beholding your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was written: To an unknown God. What, therefore, you worship without knowing, this I announce to you". But the inscription of the altar was not as Paul declared, To an unknown God, but thus: To the gods of Asia and Europe and Africa: to unknown and foreign gods. But because Paul did not need many unknown gods, but only one unknown God, he used the singular word, to teach that his God was the one whom the Athenians had inscribed in the title of the altar, and that they ought rightly to worship, knowing him, the one whom they venerated without knowing, and whom they could not fail to know. But Paul did this rarely, and as the occasion of the place rather than of display required, in the manner of bees, which are wont to make honey from various flowers and fit together the cells of the combs. There are those who think this verse was taken from Callimachus, the poet of Cyrene, and in some measure they are not mistaken. For he too, writing in praise of Jupiter against the Cretans, who boasted that they could show his tomb, says: Cretans are always liars, who even with sacrilegious mind built his tomb. But, as we said above, the whole verse was taken by the Apostle from the poet Epimenides, and Callimachus used its opening in his own poem; or else he put into meter, without theft of another's work, a common proverb by which the Cretans were called deceitful.

That Paul knew secular letters, though not to perfection, his own words testify: "One of them, a prophet of their own, said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies" (Titus 1:12). This heroic verse is by the poet Epimenides, whom both Plato and the other ancient writers recall. Among the Athenians also, when he was making his defense in the Areopagus, he added this: "As also certain of your poets have said: For we are also his offspring" (Acts 17:28). This half-line is found in Aratus, who wrote about the heaven and the stars. And also this: "Very evil conversations corrupt good morals" (1 Cor. 15:33); it is an iambic trimeter taken from a comedy of Menander. From these and other passages it is evident that Paul was not ignorant of secular letters, and that what he here called allegory he elsewhere called spiritual understanding.

Ver. 13. "Wherefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith."

This he says, because their disposition was froward, deceitful, and dissolute. They have these numberless bad qualities; and because they are prone to lying, deceiving, gluttonous, and slothful, severe reproof is necessary. For such characters will not be managed by mildness, "therefore rebuke them." He speaks not here of Gentiles, but of his own people. "Sharply." Give them, he says, a stroke that cuts deep. The Jewish tenets were fables in two ways, because they were imitations, and because the thing was past its season, for such things become fables at last. Ver. 15. "Unto the pure," he says, "all things are pure."

Thou seest that this is said to a particular purpose.

"But unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure."

Things then are not clean or unclean from their own nature, but from the disposition of him who partakes of them.

"But even their mind and conscience is defiled."

The swine therefore is clean. Why then was it forbidden as unclean? It was not unclean by nature; for, "all things are pure." Nothing is more unclean than a fish, inasmuch as it even feeds upon human flesh. But it was permitted and considered clean. Nothing is more unclean than a bird, for it eats worms; or than a stag, which is said to have its name from eating serpents. Yet all these were eaten. Why then was the swine forbidden, and many other things? Not because they were unclean, but to check excessive luxury. But had this been said, they would not have been persuaded; they were restrained therefore by the fear of uncleanness. For tell me, if we enquire nicely into these things, what is more unclean than wine; or than water, with which they mostly purified themselves? They touched not the dead, and yet they were cleansed by the dead, for the victim was dead, and with that they were cleansed. This therefore was a doctrine for children. In the composition of wine, does not dung form a part? For as the vine draws moisture from the earth, so does it from the dung that is thrown upon it. In short, if we wish to be very nice, everything is unclean, otherwise if we please not to be nice, nothing is unclean. Yet all things are pure. God made nothing unclean, for nothing is unclean, except sin only. For that reaches to the soul, and defiles it. Other uncleanness is human prejudice.

"But unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled."

For how can there be anything unclean among the pure? But he that has a weak soul makes everything unclean, and if there be set abroad a scrupulous enquiry into what is clean or unclean, he will touch nothing. For even these things are not clean, I speak of fish, and other things, according to their notions; (for "their mind and conscience," he says, "is defiled,") but all are impure. Yet Paul says not so; he turns the whole matter upon themselves. For nothing is unclean, he says, but themselves, their mind and their conscience; and nothing is more unclean than these; but an evil will is unclean.

All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and to unbelievers nothing is clean: but both their mind and their conscience are polluted. Because he had said above, "For there are many who are also not submissive, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those who are of the circumcision", and of those who had been deceived by them he had consequently added, "Rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not giving heed to Jewish fables and the commandments of men who turn themselves away from the truth"; and because, as is argued most fully to the Galatians and to the Romans, they thought there was a distinction among foods, since some seemed clean and some unclean, he therefore now adds: All things are clean to the clean, that is, to those who believe in Christ and know that every creature is good, and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving. But to the defiled and to unbelievers nothing is clean: because both their mind and their conscience are polluted; and for this reason even the things which are clean by nature become unclean to them. Not that anything is either clean or unclean, but that, according to the character of those who eat, it becomes both clean to the clean and unclean to the defiled. Otherwise, even the bread of blessing and the Lord's cup do not help any who are unbelievers and polluted; because whoever eats of that bread and drinks of the cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself (1 Cor. 11). By the coming of Christ all things have been purified. What he has cleansed, we cannot make common. But we must take care, in treating these things, not to give occasion to that heresy which, according to the Apocalypse (ch. 2) and the apostle Paul himself writing to the Corinthians, thinks one may eat of things sacrificed to idols, because all things are clean to the clean (1 Cor. 8). For the Apostle's purpose here was not to discuss the things that are sacrificed to demons, but to argue against the Jews, who, according to the discipline of the abolished Law, thought some things clean and some unclean. "For we cannot," he says, "partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons; nor can we drink at once the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons" (1 Cor. 10:20, 21). It lies with us, then, to eat things either clean or unclean. For if we are clean, the creature is clean to us. But if we are unclean and unbelievers, all things become common to us, whether through heresy dwelling in our hearts, or through the consciousness of offenses. But if our conscience does not reproach us, and we have the confidence of piety toward the Lord, we will pray with the spirit, we will pray also with the mind; we will sing with the spirit, we will sing also with the mind (1 Cor. 14); and we shall be far from those of whom it is now written: Both their mind and their conscience are polluted.

It becomes us therefore to understand the nature of things pure, and things unclean.

They confess that they know God, but in deeds they deny him: detestable, and disobedient, and reprobate for every good work. These, whose mind and conscience are polluted, confess that they know God, but in deeds deny him, according to that which is said in Isaiah: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" (Isa. 29:13). Just as, therefore, one who honors with the lips and withdraws far off with the heart, so one who confesses God in speech denies him by works. And one who denies God by works, with a feigned confession, is rightly detestable and profane; and, persuaded by no reasoning of the truth, he is called disobedient and unbelieving. Hence it comes about that he is reprobate for every good work: namely, that even the things that, overcome by natural goodness, he may perhaps have done well are not good, since they are reprobate through the perversity of his mind. Some think that God is denied only if someone, seized by the Gentiles in persecution, refuses to own himself a Christian. But see, the Apostle declares that God is denied by all deeds that are perverse. Christ is wisdom, righteousness, truth, holiness, fortitude. Wisdom is denied by folly, righteousness by iniquity, truth by lying, holiness by shamefulness, fortitude by weakness of soul. And as often as we are overcome by vices and sins, so often do we deny God; so that, on the contrary, as often as we do something well, we confess God. Nor should it be thought that on the day of judgment only those will be denied by the Son of God who denied Christ in martyrdom; but through all works, words and thoughts, Christ either, being denied, denies, or, being confessed, confesses. Of this confession, I think, he also gave command to the disciples, saying: "You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8), so that in all good works and words the mind devoted to him may confess Christ. There is also a certain praiseworthy denial, of which the Apostle himself says: "That, denying impiety and worldly desires, we may live purely and justly and piously in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of our Savior God" (Titus 2:12). Whoever denies with this denial, and is willing to follow the Savior when he says, "Whoever will come to me, let him deny himself" (Luke 9:23), having put off the old man with his works and put on the new, will follow his God. But how one denies himself must be considered. The chaste man denies the fornicator that he formerly was; the wise man the imprudent, the just man the unjust, the brave man the weak. And, to speak of all in common, we deny ourselves as often as, trampling on our former vices, we cease to be what we were and begin to be what we were not before.
SERMONS 269.4

All the heresies … they all say, "Jesus is Lord." And he's not, of course, going to eliminate from the kingdom of heaven those whom he finds to be in the Holy Spirit; and yet he did say, "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter into the kingdom of heaven." But: "Nobody can say: Jesus is Lord, except in the Holy Spirit"; nobody at all, evidently; but in the sense in which it was meant, that is in deeds.… The same apostle, you see, also says of some people, "They claim to know the Lord but deny it by their deeds." As it can be denied by deeds, so it can be said by deeds.
Sermon 36 On the Feast of the Epiphany, 6

Our state of peace, therefore, dearly-beloved, has its dangers, and it is vain for those who do not withstand vicious desires to feel secure of the liberty which is the privilege of their Faith. Men's hearts are shown by the character of their works, and the fashion of their minds is betrayed by the nature of their actions. For there are some, as the Apostle says, "who profess that they know God, but deny Him by their deeds." For the charge of denial is truly incurred when the good which is heard in the sound of the voice is not present in the conscience. Indeed, the frailty of man's nature easily glides into faults.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 19

"For many are called, but few are chosen," because many come to faith, yet few are led to the heavenly kingdom. For behold, how many of us have gathered for today's feast, we fill the walls of the Church, yet who knows how few there are who are numbered in that flock of God's elect? For behold, the voice of all proclaims Christ, but the life of all does not proclaim Him. Most follow God with their voices, but flee from Him by their conduct. Hence Paul says: "They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny Him." Hence James says: "Faith without works is dead." Hence through the Psalmist the Lord says: "I have declared and spoken, they have multiplied beyond number." For when the Lord calls, the faithful are multiplied beyond number, because sometimes even those come to faith who do not attain to the number of the elect. For here they are mingled with the faithful through confession, but because of their reprobate life they do not deserve to be numbered there in the lot of the faithful.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 26

What greatly gladdens is what follows: "Blessed are they who have not seen and have believed." In this saying, we are indeed specially marked out, we who retain in our minds Him whom we have not seen in the flesh. We are marked out—but only if we follow our faith with works. For he truly believes who practices by his deeds what he believes. In contrast to these, concerning those who hold faith in name only, Paul says: "They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny Him." Hence James says: "Faith without works is dead."
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 29

"He who believes and is baptized shall be saved, but he who does not believe shall be condemned." Perhaps each one may say within himself: "I have already believed; I shall be saved." He speaks truly, if he holds faith by works. For true faith is that which does not contradict in conduct what it says in words. Hence it is that Paul says of certain false believers: "They profess to know God, but they deny Him by their deeds." Hence John says: "He who says he knows God and does not keep His commandments is a liar." Since this is so, we ought to recognize the truth of our faith in the consideration of our life. For then we are truly faithful, if we fulfill in works what we promise in words.

n: Sound doctrine. It is not sufficient to teach sound doctrine, says St. Jerome, if it be not at the same time taught in a manner worthy of itself; that is, if he who teaches it by his words belies it in his actions. (St. Jerome)

Be sober. The Greek Fathers, Theodoret, and Theophylactus, translate the word, sober, attentive, or vigilant. But Latin interpreters understand it of sobriety, in the literal meaning of the word. Old men oftentimes under pretense of weakness, drink wine to excess. The ancients called wine the milk of old men; hence aquilœ senectus has passed into a proverb, to designate an old man who drinks much and eats little. (Calmet)

In holy attire.[1] See 1 Timothy ii. 9. The Greek word is sometimes used to signify the whole constitution, or state of a man's health in all the parts of his body: here it is taken for a woman's whole exterior carriage, her gait, gesture, looks, discourse, dress, that nothing appear but what is edifying. (Witham)

Love their husbands. This is the first lesson he wishes to be given to young women; that they should always manifest a love, an attachment, respect and obedience to their husbands. But it must be a chaste love. Vult eas amare viros suos castè; vult inter virum et mulierem esse pudicam dilectionem. (St. Jerome)
Discreet, chaste, sober. In the Greek is nothing for sober. The Latin interpreter seems to have added it, as another signification of one of the Greek words. See 1 Timothy iii. 2. (Witham)

In gravity: to which is added in the Protestant translation sincerity,[2] from some Greek copies; but it is left out by Dr. Wells, as being not in the best Greek manuscripts nor is it in the Amsterdam edition, (1711.) (Witham)

Servants to be obedient. Servants owe respect and submission to their masters in every thing not contrary to the law, or the will of God. Hence they are strictly forbidden to murmur at their commands, to show any repugnance to obey them, or to censure their conduct. To avoid these evils, they ought to consider their masters as Jesus Christ himself, and their commands as those of God himself: which St. Paul often inculcates in other places in his epistles. (Ephesians vi. 5, 6.; Colossians iii. 23.) (St. Jerome)

Not defrauding.[3] St. Jerome puts, not stealing. The Greek signifies private thefts. Dr. Wells, not by filching. --- That they may adorn (or give honour to) the doctrine of God, our Saviour, in all things; by whom we may understand God, i.e. Christ, God and Man, or God as common to the three divine persons. (Witham) --- Thus ought they to shew forth in their whole conduct that strict love of justice and sanctity which the Catholic faith inspires into those who profess it, and live up to the admirable rules it prescribes; thus alone can they be said to do honour to their religion, when they practically perform what they speculatively believe.
For the grace of God, our Saviour, hath appeared to all men. In the Greek: For the saving grace of God, &c. (Witham)

We should live soberly,[4] and justly, and piously. St. Jerome puts (as in other places for the same Greek word) chastely, justly, and piously. The words comprehend man's duty to himself, to his neighbour, and towards God. (Witham)

Waiting for the blessed hope; for the happiness of the blessed in heaven, promised and hoped for. --- And coming of the glory of the great God,[5] and our Saviour Jesus Christ. The title of great God, says Dr. Wells, is here referred to our Saviour Jesus Christ, by Clement of Alexandria in protreptico, chap. vi. He might have added, and by the general consent of the Greek and Latin Fathers. St. Chrysostom cries out: "where are now they who say that the Son is less than the Father?" St. Jerome in like manner: "where is the serpent Arius? where is the snake Eunomius?" And that this title of great God is here given to Jesus Christ, may be shewn from the text itself, especially in the Greek; for the glorious coming, and appearance, in other places of St. Paul, is always used to signify Christ's coming to judge the world. Secondly, inasmuch as one and the same Greek article falls upon the great God, and our Saviour Christ; so that even M. Simon, in a note on these words, says the construction is, and the coming of Jesus Christ, the great God, our Saviour, and blames Erasmus and Grotius for pretending that this place is not a confutation of the Arians. (Witham)

He says in the Septuagint it corresponds to segula, which signifies a man's proper possessions, which he has purchased or chosen for himself. f: Homily on Titus 3

ii. 1. "But speak thou the things that become sound doctrine."

This then is uncleanness. They are themselves unclean. But be not thou silent on that account. Do thy part, although they may not receive thee. Advise and counsel them, though they may not be persuaded. Here he censures them more severely. For they who are mad imagine that nothing stands still, yet this arises not from the objects that are seen, but from the eyes that see. Because they are unsteady and giddy, they think that the earth turns round with them, which yet turns not, but stands firm. The derangement is of their own state, not from any affection of the element. So it is here, when the soul is unclean, it thinks all things unclean. Therefore scrupulous observances are no mark of purity, but it is the part of purity to be bold in all things. For he that is pure by nature ventures upon all things, they that are defiled, upon nothing. This we may say against Marcion. Seest thou that it is a mark of purity to be superior to all defilement, to touch nothing implies impurity. This holds even with respect to God. That He assumed flesh is a proof of purity; if through fear He had not taken it, there would have been defilement. He who eats not things that seem unclean, is himself unclean and weak, he who eats, is neither. Let us not call such pure, they are the unclean. He is pure, who dares to feed upon all things. All this caution we ought to exercise towards the things that defile the soul. For that is uncleanness, that is defilement. None of these things is so. Those who have a vitiated palate think what is set before them is unclean, but this is the effect of their disorder. It becomes us therefore to understand the nature of things pure, and things unclean.
Commentary on Titus

But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine. It is one thing to speak sound doctrine, another to teach the things that suit sound doctrine: for in the one there is simple instruction only; in the other, together with the teaching, there is also the correction of life. "For whoever breaks one of these least commandments, and teaches men so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 5:19): the Lord commanding the disciples that they ought not only to labor in meditation on the Scriptures, so as to go over what is written and store it up in the treasury of memory, but first to do what has been commanded. "But whoever does and teaches, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." For unless our righteousness surpasses the righteousness of the scribes and of the Pharisees, we cannot enter the kingdoms of heaven (Matt. 5). They, sitting upon the chair of Moses, say and do not do, and bind unbearable burdens which they lay upon men's necks, and will not themselves touch them with their least finger. This, then, is what the Apostle now teaches Titus, his son in Christ and his disciple: to speak the things that suit sound doctrine; because doctrine has soundness then, when the teacher's doctrine and his life agree alike.
Homily on Titus 4

There are some failings which age has, that youth has not. Some indeed it has in common with youth, but in addition it has a slowness, a timidity, a forgetfulness, an insensibility, and an irritability. For this reason he exhorts old men concerning these matters, "to be vigilant." For there are many things which at this period make men otherwise than vigilant, especially what I mentioned, their general insensibility, and the difficulty of stirring or exciting them. Wherefore he also adds, "grave, temperate." Here he means prudent. For temperance is named from the well-tempered mind. For there are, indeed there are, among the old, some who rave and are beside themselves, some from wine, and some from sorrow. For old age makes them narrowminded.

"Sound in faith, in charity [love], in patience."

He has well added "in patience," for this quality more especially befits old men.
Commentary on Titus

That old men be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, and in love, and in patience. Having first commanded Titus in general what he himself ought to say to all, where he says, "But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine", he now sets out, class by class, what befits each age. First what suits old men, then what befits old women, third what is fitting for the young, both male, that is, and female; although within the precept for the old women he has set down the commands concerning young women, so that he did not so much teach the young women himself as set out what they should be taught by the old women. Lastly he speaks of slaves; and through each age and condition he lays down his precepts so fittingly that his speech is a rule of life and of morals. Old men, then, are to be sober, or watchful, because νηφάλιοι among the Greeks means both; honorable, so that gravity of morals may adorn the gravity of age; chaste, lest they run riot at an age not suited to it, lest, with blood already cold toward lust, they be an example to the young unto ruin. Sound in faith: of this soundness of faith we spoke above. And sound not only in faith but also in love and in patience, so that, when they have first the soundness of faith, they may hear from the Savior: "Your faith has made you whole" (Mark 10:52). And elsewhere: "For not even in Israel have I found such faith" (Matt. 8:10). And because of this same soundness of faith let them become sons of Abraham, of whom it is written: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness" (Gen. 15:6). And Habakkuk, recalling this soundness of faith, says: "But the just man lives by my faith" (Hab. 2:4). Read again the Epistle of the apostle Paul to the Hebrews (or of whoever else you think it is, since it has now been received among the ecclesiastical writings), count through that whole catalogue of faith in which it is written: "By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain" (Heb. 11:4 ff.). And: "Enoch was translated, that he should not see death"; and Noah, believing God about the things he did not yet see, built the ark; and Abraham went out into a land he did not know. And lest Scripture should seem to give women no example of faith, it is written in the same Epistle that Sarah too received power to conceive seed when the time of her age was already past it, because she judged him faithful who had promised. There the faith of Isaac and of Jacob, of Joseph, of Moses too and of Rahab, and of the rest, is praised, whom he can know better who has read the Epistle itself. As there is, then, a soundness of faith, so the same soundness is also in love. And who possesses the soundness of love but he who has first loved God with all his soul, and with all his heart, and with all his strength? Then, hearing Christ's precept concerning his neighbor, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Matt. 5), he has divided his love: because on these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets. He who has the soundness of love is not envious, is not puffed up, does not act wrongly, not dishonorably, is not provoked to anger, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, awaits all things (1 Cor. 13). And because love never falls away, he who is in the soundness of love never himself falls either. For neither tribulation, nor distress, nor famine, nor persecution, nor nakedness, nor peril, nor sword will be able to separate him from the soundness of love which he has in Christ Jesus. Why should I speak of the sword and the other lesser things, which cannot divide him who possesses the love of soundness, when neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature whatever can separate him who has the love of soundness in Christ Jesus? If the soundness of love has been understood by us, let us take from the Scriptures some example of those who are in weakness of love. The Savior says of the last times: "Because when iniquity has been multiplied, the love of many will grow cold" (Matt. 24). For love is warm in those who are fervent in spirit, but cold, icy and frozen in those who have taken in the harshest blasts of the North wind. "For from the North evils will blaze forth upon all who inhabit the land" (Jer. 1:14). With this coldness of love Amnon too had grown stiff toward his sister Tamar (2 Sam. 13). We must fear, then, lest we too at some time be overcome by this weakness of love. For it sometimes happens that at first our love toward a virgin, or toward any woman, is holy; and when the mind has been softened into affections, little by little the soundness of love grows pale with languor, and begins to weaken, and carries the lover to final death. Hence the Apostle too, cautiously and prudently, commands Timothy to exhort the young women in all purity (1 Tim. 5). And all purity is in flesh and spirit and soul: that the eye be not made to stumble; that we not hang clinging to the beauty of a woman's face; that it not delight us to hear flattering words; that the mind, hard before, not wilt at feigned words. Let them beware, then, as we have said, young men as well as old, young women as well as old women, and keep their heart with all diligence, lest through the soundness of love the sickness of love enter in, and through holy love there come to be an unholy love which drags them down to Gehenna. Let him who is sound in faith, who is sound in love, be sound also in patience: and in patience, which is proved above all in temptations; because it profits nothing to have had the things we enumerated above, unless all the riches and merchandise with which the ship is laden are preserved in the storm, and, while the winds blow from this side and that, what has been well gained is delivered without shipwreck. "He who", indeed, "has persevered to the end, he shall be saved" (Matt. 24:13).
The Stromata Book 4

It is evident, then, in my opinion, that she will charge herself with remedying, by good sense and persuasion, each of the annoyances that originate with her husband in domestic economy. And if he do not yield, then she will endeavour, as far as possible for human nature, to lead a sinless life; whether it be necessary to die, in accordance with reason, or to live; considering that God is her helper and associate in such a course of conduct, her true defender and Saviour both for the present and for the future; making Him the leader and guide of all her actions, reckoning sobriety and righteousness her work, and making the favour of God her end. Gracefully, therefore, the apostle says in the Epistle to Titus, "that the eider women should be of godly behaviour, should not be slanderers, not enslaved to much wine; that they should counsel the young women to be lovers of their husbands, lovers of their children, discreet, chaste, housekeepers, good, subject to their own husbands; that the word of God be not blasphemed."
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 7

It wills, therefore, that these, to whom the "Lord himself is the portion", be sober, fasting, watchful at every time, but especially when they stand ready at the altars to beseech the Lord and to sacrifice in his sight. And these commandments preserve their force to such a degree, and are to be kept with all observance, that even the Apostle confirms these same things by the laws of the New Testament. In it, similarly laying down for the priests or the chiefs of priests the rules of life, he says that they ought "not" to be given to "much wine", but to be "sober". And sobriety indeed is the mother of all virtues, just as, on the contrary, drunkenness is of all vices. For the Apostle plainly declared, saying: "wine, wherein is riot", that he might show that from drunkenness, as a firstborn daughter, riot is begotten.
COMMENTARY ON 1 CORINTHIANS FRAGMENT LXXIV

And from elsewhere too I shall establish this — even though that other passage is more securely stated concerning the woman not becoming a leader of the man by speech: "aged women in demeanor reverent, teachers of what is good, that they may train the young women to be sober-minded," not simply that they may teach. For let women too be teachers of what is good, yet not so that men should sit and listen to women, as though there were a lack of men able to serve as ambassadors of the word of God.
Homily on Titus 4

Ver. 3. "The aged women likewise, that they be in behavior as becometh holiness."

That is, that in their very dress and carriage they exhibit modesty.

"Not false accusers, not given to much wine."

For this was particularly the vice of women and of old age. For from their natural coldness at that period of life arises the desire of wine, therefore he directs his exhortation to that point, to cut off all occasion of drunkenness, wishing them to be far removed from that vice, and to escape the ridicule that attends it. For the fumes mount more easily from beneath, and the membranes (of the brain) receive the mischief from their being impaired by age, and this especially causes intoxication. Yet wine is necessary at this age, because of its weakness, but much is not required. Nor do young women require much, though for a different reason, because it kindles the flame of lust.

"Teachers of good things."

And yet thou forbiddest a woman to teach; how dost thou command it here, when elsewhere thou sayest, "I suffer not a woman to teach"? (1 Tim. ii. 12.) But mark what he has added, "Nor to usurp authority over the man." For at the beginning it was permitted to men to teach both men and women. But to women it is allowed to instruct by discourse at home. But they are nowhere permitted to preside, nor to extend their speech to great length, wherefore he adds, "Nor to usurp authority over the man."
Commentary on Titus

Old women likewise in holy demeanor, not inciters, not enslaved to much wine; teaching well, that they may instruct the young women in purity, that they may love their husbands, that they may love their children: chaste, pure, having care of the house, kind, subject to their husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed. Although the apostle Peter has commanded that husbands give honor to their wives as to the weaker vessel, it is not, however, to be supposed that a wife, who has a weak vessel of the body, is at once weaker in soul as well. Hence it is now commanded them, so that in them too that saying of the Apostle may be fulfilled: "Power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor. 12:9); and it is said that they also are to have all the things that were commanded in common to the old men, namely in that he says, Old women likewise, that is, just as the old men, honorable in all things, sober, chaste, sound in faith, and in love, and in patience; and, for their sex, they are to have this as their own, that they be in holy demeanor, or, as it reads better in the Greek, ἐν καταστήματι ἱεροπρεπεῖς (in a bearing befitting what is sacred), so that their very gait and movement, face, speech and silence may display a certain dignity of sacred seemliness. And because this kind of little women is usually talkative, according to that saying: "And at the same time, being idle, they learn to go about from house to house; and not only idle, but also wordy and busybodies, speaking things they ought not" (1 Tim. 5:13): therefore he wants them to be not inciters (incentrices), that is, not accusers, not such as disparage some in order to please others. Or certainly, not such as, because they themselves have already passed beyond youth, discuss the ages of the young women and say: That one adorns herself so, that one does her hair so, so that one goes out; she loves him, she is loved by him: whereas, even if these things are true, they ought not so much to accuse her before the others as to reprove the girl herself in private with the love of Christ, and rather to teach her not to do it than to accuse in public what she has done. Women of this age, because they have grown cold to the licentiousness of the body (although there are very many who are not ashamed of their gray hairs, and, trembling, are dressed up as little maidens before a flock of grandchildren), are accustomed to give themselves to wine in place of lust; and when among their cups they have seemed to themselves wise and eloquent, to put on a kind of austerity of morals, speaking as what they seem to themselves to be, and not remembering what they were. So let old women be kept also from too much drinking of wine, since what lust is in the young, drunkenness is in the old. Or how can an old woman teach young women purity, when, if a young woman has imitated the drunkenness of an old woman, she cannot be chaste? And he expressed it pointedly: not enslaved to much wine. For it is a kind of servitude, and the lowest condition, for a man's senses to be seized by wine, and for him to be not his own but wine's. Since, then, he taught first what the old women ought to be, and after the things they have in common with the old men set out also the things proper to them, that they be full of an honorable and holy demeanor and of all seemliness: not accusers, not disparaging others, not with their senses seized by wine; now, accordingly, he hands them the reins of teaching, so that, when they are such, they may have freedom to teach, namely to teach the things that are good. For although in another place he has said, "But I do not permit women to teach" (1 Tim. 2:12), it must be understood thus: that teaching directed at men is taken from them. For the rest, let them teach the young women as their daughters.
Homily on Titus 4

Ver. 4. "That they may teach the young women to be sober."

Observe how he binds the people together, how he subjects the younger women to the elder. For he is not speaking there of daughters, but merely in respect of age. Let each of the elder women, he means, teach any one that is younger to be sober.

"To love their husbands."

This is the chief point of all that is good in a household, "A man and his wife that agree together." (Ecclus. xxv. 1.) For where this exists, there will be nothing that is unpleasant. For where the head is in harmony with the body, and there is no disagreement between them, how shall not all the other members be at peace? For when the rulers are at peace, who is there to divide and break up concord? as on the other hand, where these are ill disposed to each other, there will be no good order in the house. This then is a point of the highest importance, and of more consequence than wealth, or rank, or power, or aught else. Nor has he said merely to be at peace, but "to love their husbands." For where love is, no discord will find admittance, far from it, other advantages too spring up.

"To love their children." This is well added, since she who loves the root, will much more love the fruit.

"To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good." All these spring from love. They become "good, and keepers at home," from affection to their husbands.

"Obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed."

She who despises her husband, neglects also her house; but from love springs great soberness, and all contention is done away. And if he be a Heathen, he will soon be persuaded; and if he be a Christian, he will become a better man. Seest thou the condescension of Paul? He who in everything would withdraw us from worldly concerns, here bestows his consideration upon domestic affairs. For when these are well conducted, there will be room for spiritual things, but otherwise, they too will be marred. For she who keeps at home will be also sober, she that keeps at home will be also a prudent manager, she will have no inclination for luxury, unseasonable expenses, and other such things.

"That the word of God," he says, "be not blasphemed."

See how his first concern is for the preaching of the word, not for worldly things; for when he writes to Timothy, he says, "that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty" (1 Tim. ii. 2); and here, "that the word of God," and the doctrine, "be not blasphemed." For if it should happen that a believing woman, married to an unbeliever, should not be virtuous, the blasphemy is usually carried on to God; but if she be of good character, the Gospel obtains glory from her, and from her virtuous actions. Let those women hearken who are united to wicked men or unbelievers; let them hear, and learn to lead them to godliness by their own example. For if thou gain nothing else, and do not attract thy husband to embrace right doctrines, yet thou hast stopped his mouth, and dost not allow him to blaspheme Christianity; and this is no mean thing, but great indeed, that the doctrine should be admired through our conversation.
Commentary on Titus

First purity: because the enemy fights more against this in the flowering age, and all his power against women is in the navel of the belly; then that they love their husbands and love their children. What teaching is there in loving husbands, since this is established not in the eloquence of one who teaches but in the heart of one who loves? He wants them to love their husbands purely: he wants there to be a chaste love between husband and wife, so that with modesty and reserve, and as if by the necessity of her sex, she rather renders the debt to her husband than herself demands it of him, and believes that she performs the work of begetting children before the eyes of God and of the angels: thus she will not blush even at the secret couch, and the darkness of the night, and her closed chamber, since she will have reflected that all things lie open to the eyes of God. And they love their children thus, if they instruct them in the discipline of God. But to be unwilling to sadden them by teaching the things that are good, and to grant them the freedom to sin, is not to love children but to hate them.
Commentary on Titus

Let the young women also be instructed to have care of the house. And because it could happen that the care of the house was governed with harshness, and through this precept of the Apostle the matron might become too severe toward the household servants, he therefore joined to it kind: so that she might believe that she rules her husband's house well when she commands the servants with kindness, not with terror. And also subject to their husbands: lest, puffed up by riches and rank, they not remember the sentence of God by which they are subjected to their husbands. For he says to the woman: "Your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you" (Gen. 3:16). In this the prudence of holy Scripture is to be considered: that the Lord did not say this to the man, saying, "You shall rule over your wife", but to the woman herself, so as to leave her the reward of compliance, since it is in her own power, if she wishes to obey the precepts of God, to serve the man and to be subject to her husband, so that it might in some way be a free servitude, and full of love; she is therefore serving her husband while she fears to offend him. For man was not created for the woman, but woman for the man. And since the man is the head of the woman, and Christ the head of the man, any wife who is not subject to her husband, that is, to her head, is guilty of the same crime as the man is if he is not subject to Christ, his head. And the word of the Lord is blasphemed either when the first sentence of God is despised and counted for nothing, or when the Gospel of Christ is defamed, while she who is a Christian, and subject by the law of God, desires, against the law and the faith of nature, to command her husband: when even Gentile women serve their husbands by the common law of nature.
Homily on Titus 4

Ver. 6. "Young men likewise exhort to be soberminded."

See how he everywhere recommends the observance of decorum. For he has committed to women the greater part in the instruction of women, having appointed the elder to teach the younger. But the whole instruction of men he assigns to Titus himself. For nothing is so difficult for that age as to overcome unlawful pleasures. For neither the love of wealth, nor the desire of glory, or any other thing so much solicits the young, as fleshly lust. Therefore passing over other things, he directs his admonition to that vital point. Not however that he would have other things neglected; for what says he?
Commentary on Titus

Exhort the young men likewise to be chaste in all things, showing yourself an example of good works, in doctrine, in integrity and purity, in sound and irreprehensible speech, so that he who is on the opposing side may be abashed, having nothing evil to say of us. Just as, in what he had commanded above, saying, "Old women likewise in holy demeanor", we had said that the likeness of the old women was to be referred to the old men, so now, in what he has added, "Urge the young men likewise to be chaste", we judge that the likeness of the young men is to be fitted to the old women, and through the old women to the old men: so that they have the sobriety of the old men, and be honorable and chaste, and sound in faith, and in love, and in patience; and that of the old women in holiness of demeanor, that they be not accusers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching well, and the rest. And he has set down this as proper to the young men, that they be chaste in all things, namely in mind as well as in body, in deed as well as in thought, so that there be in a young man no suspicion of shamefulness. And although some of the Latins think it should be read thus: "Urge the young men likewise to be chaste", and afterward add, "in all things showing yourself a pattern of good works", yet let us know that in all things is to be referred to what precedes, that is: urge them to be chaste in all things. It must also be known that continence is necessary not only in the work of the flesh and in the desire of the mind, but in all things: that we may not seek undue honors, that we may not be inflamed by avarice, that we may not be overcome by any passion.
The Canonical Epistle

For when the blessed apostle Paul had undergone many persecutions, and had shown forth the prizes of many contests, though he knew that it was far better to "depart, and to be with Christ," yet he brings this forward, and says, "Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you." For considering not his own advantage but the advantage of many, that they might be saved, he judged it more necessary than his own rest to remain with the brethren, and to have a care for them; who also would have him that teacheth to be "in doctrine" an example to the faithful.
ON THE TRINITY 8.1

Accordingly he has provided Titus, the person to whom his words were addressed, with an injunction as to the perfect practice of religion to this effect: "In all things shewing thyself an ensample of good works, teaching with gravity sound words that cannot be condemned, that the adversary may be ashamed, having nothing disgraceful or evil to say of us." This teacher of the Gentiles and elect doctor of the Church, from his consciousness of Christ who spoke and dwelt within him, knew well that the infection of tainted speech would spread abroad, and that the corruption of pestilent doctrine would furiously rage against the sound form of faithful words, and infusing the poison of its own evil tenets into the inmost soul, would creep on with deep-seated mischief. For it is of these that he says, "Whose word spreadeth like a cancer," tainting the health of the mind, invaded by it with a secret and stealthy contagion. For this reason, he wished that there should be in the bishop the teaching of sound words, a good conscience in the faith and expertness in exhortation to withstand wicked and false and wild gainsayings.
Homily on Titus 4

Ver. 7. "In all things showing thyself a pattern of good works."

Let the elder women, he says, teach the younger, but do thou thyself exhort young men to be soberminded. And let the luster of thy life be a common school of instruction, a pattern of virtue to all, publicly exhibited, like some original model, containing in itself all beauties, affording examples whence those who are willing may easily imprint upon themselves any of its excellences.

Ver. 7, 8. "In [thy] doctrine showing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity, Sound speech that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you."

By "him that is of the contrary part," he means the devil, and every one who ministers to him. For when the life is illustrious, and the discourse corresponds to it, being meek and gentle, and affording no handle to the adversaries, it is of unspeakable advantage. Of great use then is the ministry of the word, not any common word, but that which is approved, and cannot be condemned, affording no pretext to those who are willing to censure it.
Commentary on Titus

"Showing yourself", he says, "a pattern of good works". It profits nothing for someone to be practiced in speaking and to have worn his tongue smooth for talking, unless he teaches more by example than by word. In short, one who is unchaste, however eloquent he may be, if he exhorts his hearers to purity, his speech is weak and has no authority to exhort. And conversely, however rustic and slow of speech he may be, if he is pure, he can by his example drive men to the likeness of his life. And what he says, "in incorruption", is to be taken thus: that incorruption (incorruptio) properly means virginity. Indeed, those who are virgins are commonly called incorrupt (incorrupti), and those who have ceased to be virgins are named corrupted (corrupti); and we say: She who was once a virgin has been corrupted. Hence I think that Titus, believing the Gospel before he was taken up with the work of the flesh, received baptism and remained a virgin, and is now admonished by the Apostle to show a pattern of himself in incorruption: an incorruption which, indeed, we do not see in Timothy. For when he said to him, "Let no one despise your youth, but be a pattern of the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity" (1 Tim. 4:12), he was silent about incorruption and set down only "purity". But purity can be understood also in celibacy without virginity. Unless perhaps we take purity as in the mind, and incorruption as in the body, according to what is written elsewhere in the definition of a virgin: "That she may be holy in body and in spirit" (1 Cor. 7). And he himself has now added in sequence: "in doctrine, in incorruption, in chastity". We could interpret both chastity and incorruption as the integrity of doctrine too, were it not that what follows specifically, sound and irreprehensible speech, would then hold a precept of its own concerning instruction in doctrine.
Sermons 355.1

As far as we are concerned, our consciences are all that matters. As far as you are concerned, our reputation among you ought not to be tarnished but influential for good. Mark what I've said, and make the distinction. There are two things, conscience and reputation; conscience for yourself, reputation for your neighbor. Those who, being clear in their consciences, neglect their reputations, are being cruel; especially if they find themselves in this position. The apostle writes about this to his disciple: "Showing yourself to all around you as an example of good works."
Commentary on Titus

And as for his saying irreprehensible speech: not that anyone is of such eloquence and prudence as to be reprehended by no one (for even the apostles and evangelists are reprehended by heretics and Gentiles), but that he says or does nothing worthy of reprehension, even though adversaries are ready to reprehend. And because there are many who are not subject, empty talkers and deceivers of minds, who hate him who reproves in the gates and abhor holy speech, therefore let us show ourselves an example in all things, in doctrine, in integrity, in chastity, in sound and irreprehensible speech, so that our adversaries, thoroughly frightened by the soundness of our life and doctrine, may not dare to accuse, that is, may fabricate nothing plausible in accusation. And indeed to this day we see some in the churches (although this is a rare bird) of such gravity and continence that they have testimony even from their adversaries, and it is said: That man is great, and of holy conduct and upright morals, were he not a heretic. For no one is of such unbounded impudence that he could accuse the rays of the sun of being dark, and overspread its clear light with the gloom of night. Hence the Apostle too, guarding against these same things, says: "That I may cut off occasion from those who desire occasion" (2 Cor. 11:12). He who is on the opposing side can also be understood as the devil, who is the accuser of our brethren, as John the Evangelist proclaims: who, when he has nothing evil to lay against us, blushes, and the slanderer will not be able to slander. And diabolus in the Latin language means "slanderer" (criminator).
Homily on Titus 4

Ver. 9. "Exhort servants to be obedient to their own masters, and to please them well in all things."

Dost thou see what he has previously said, "that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you." He therefore is deserving of condemnation, who under pretense of continence separates wives from their husbands, and he who under any other pretext takes away servants from their masters. This is not "speech that cannot be condemned," but it gives great handle to the unbelieving, and opens the mouths of all against us.

"Not answering again."

Ver. 10. "Not purloining, but showing all good fidelity, that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things."

Thus he has well said in another place, "Doing service as to the Lord, and not to men." For if thou servest thy master with good will, yet the occasion of this service proceeds from thy fear, and he who with so great fear renders Him service, shall receive the greater reward. For if he restrain not his hand, or his unruly tongue, how shall the Gentile admire the doctrine that is among us? But if they see their slave, who has been taught the philosophy of Christ, displaying more self-command than their own philosophers, and serving with all meekness and good will, he will in every way admire the power of the Gospel. For the Greeks judge not of doctrines by the doctrine itself, but they make the life and conduct the test of the doctrines. Let women therefore and servants be their instructors by their conversation.

"Not purloining, but showing all good fidelity, that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things."

When therefore it is seen that the power of religion, imposing a restraint upon a class naturally so self-willed, has rendered them singularly well behaved and gentle, their masters, however unreasonable they may be, will form a high opinion of our doctrines. For it is manifest, that having previously infixed in their souls a fear of the Resurrection, of the Judgment, and of all those things which we are taught by our philosophy to expect after death, they have been able to resist wickedness, having in their souls a settled principle to counterbalance the pleasures of sin. So that it is not by chance or without reason, that Paul shows so much consideration for this class of men: since the more wicked they are, the more admirable is the power of that preaching which reforms them. For we then most admire a physician, when he restores to a healthy and sane state one who was despaired of, whom nothing benefited, who was unable to command his unreasonable desires, and wallowed in them. And observe what he most requires of them; the qualities which contribute most to their masters' ease.

"Not answering again, not purloining"; that is, to show all good will in matters intrusted to them, to be particularly faithful in their masters' concerns, and obedient to their commands.
Commentary on Titus

Let slaves be subject to their masters in all things: let them be pleasing, not contradicting, not stealing, but showing all good faith, that they may adorn the doctrine of our Savior, God, in all things. Since our Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel, "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you" (Matt. 11:28), considers no condition, age or sex a stranger to blessedness, therefore the Apostle now lays down precepts for slaves too, namely as for a part of the Church and members of the body of Christ. And just as above he taught what Titus ought to instruct the old men, the old women, the young women and the young men, so now he lays down precepts suited to slaves. First, that they be subject to their masters in all things. But in all those things which are not contrary to God: so that if the master commands things that are not opposed to the holy Scriptures, the slave is to be subject to the master; but if he commands things contrary to them, let him obey the master of the spirit rather than the master of the body. Pay careful attention to how he decrees precepts suited to the persons. "Let slaves", he says, "be subject to their masters in all things" (Eph. 6:5). In another place, treating of children, he says: "Children, obey your parents" (Col. 3:20). For it befits children to obey their parents, but slaves to be subject to a master who commands. Nor let us think it contradictory that in another Epistle "Let wives", he says, "be subject to their husbands" (Eph. 5:22; Col. 3:18), and in this one has declared that wives are to be subject to their husbands, as though he used the same word both of slaves and of wives. For in a certain way the husband is the master of the wife. "He", it says, "shall rule over you" (Gen. 3:16). The Savior too was subject to his parents (Luke 2), but when he was still twelve years old and differed in nothing from a slave, though Lord of all; for he had not yet reached the full age of a man that could take up the inheritance. But it is also written of him elsewhere: "For when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to himself, that God may be all in all" (1 Cor. 15:28). And all things will be subjected to him when he has said, "The Lord to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet" (Ps. 109:1). In slaves who are subject, the Lord is subject. And just as he is said to be a curse for us, though he is not a curse but true blessing, so for us he is written either as subject or as not subject, according as we are either subject to God or not subject. Some read this passage thus: Let slaves be subject to their masters, and after they have punctuated up to here, they add, in all things let them please: whereas in the Greek the order of the reading is different, that is, let slaves be subject to their masters in all things; so that there follows εὐαρέστους εἶναι, which we can render, though not fully, yet in some measure, that they be well content with themselves: namely, lest the sentence of God on their condition should seem unjust to them. But just as the poor man can be saved according to his measure, and the woman in the weakness of her sex is not excluded from the kingdom of God, and every condition can attain blessedness according to its rank, so let slaves too be well content with themselves that they are slaves, and not think that they cannot serve God because they are subject to men; but rather that they please the will of God in this, if they are both subject to their masters in all things and well content with themselves in their condition; and let them carry out what the Apostle commands next, that they be not contradicting, not stealing. Indeed the greatest vice of slaves is to contradict their masters, and, when these have commanded anything, to mutter to themselves. Therefore he admonishes Titus to take away, through sound doctrine, a passion of this kind from those who are Christian slaves. For if the slave must carry out what the master commands, why should he not do this very thing with good will, rather than both offend his master and still do what he is told: especially since God too was offended at the water of contradiction? And in another place he speaks of the murmuring people: "Let their murmuring cease from me, and they shall not die" (Num. 17).
SERMONS 94

A bishopric necessarily pertains to him who is the head of the household. It is a superintendence of the faith of the members of the household, lest any fall into heresy. It extends to the wife, to a son or a daughter; it extends also to a slave, for he has also been redeemed at so great a price. The apostolic teaching assumes the placement of the master above the slave and the slave beneath the master, but Christ has given the same price for each of them. Do not neglect even the lowliest among your household.
Commentary on Titus

After contradiction, let the doctrine of Christ correct another vice of slaves too, "that they be not thieves". Now a thief is judged one not only in greater things but also in lesser. For it is not what has been carried off by theft but the mind of the one stealing that is considered. Just as in fornication and adultery, the fornication or adultery is not different on this account, if the woman is beautiful or rich, ugly or poor, a harlot or an adulteress, but whatever she may be, it is one fornication, or adultery: so also in theft, however much a slave has carried off, he incurs the crime of theft. Hence in the law of Moses thieves are compelled sometimes to restore sevenfold, sometimes fourfold, and at times the thief himself is cut down, at times he is sold for his theft, matters which I recall that I recently expounded to you in Leviticus. But if this is forbidden in a slave, how much more in a free man, lest either a judge plunder, or a soldier not content with his pay lay waste what belongs to others? Finely did a certain man of the greatest gravity, when the integrity of a certain judge was being praised to him and the one praising said of him, "He is not a thief", reply: "He would make an excellent slave, if he were not a runaway as well": so far should the suspicion of theft be from every free man. So let slaves be subject to their masters in all things, let them be well content with their condition, so that they do not bear slavery bitterly, do not contradict their masters, do not steal, and besides this show good faith in all things, that they may adorn the doctrine of the Savior, our God, in all things. For if they have been faithful in the least with their fleshly masters, greater things will begin to be entrusted to them with God. And he adorns the doctrine of the Lord who does the things that are fitting to his condition. And on the other hand he puts it to confusion who is not subject in all things, whose condition displeases him, who, a contradicter and a defrauder, shows good faith in nothing. For how can he be faithful with the goods of God who could not show faith to a fleshly master?
Catechetical Lecture 15:2-3

For Paul has also shown us that there are these two comings, in his epistle to Titus where he says, "The grace of God our Savior has appeared unto all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously and godly in this present world; looking for that blessed hope and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ." You note how he acknowledges with thanksgiving the first coming and that we look for a second.… So our Lord Jesus Christ comes from heaven and comes with glory at the last day to bring this world to its close.
Homily on Titus 5

Having demanded from servants so great virtue, for it is great virtue to adorn the doctrine of our God and Saviour in all things, and charged them to give no occasion of offense to their masters, even in common matters, he adds the just cause, why servants should be such: "For the grace of God, that bringeth salvation, hath appeared." Those who have God for their Teacher, may well be such as I have described, seeing their numberless sins have been forgiven to them. For you know that in addition to other considerations, this in no common degree awes and humbles the soul, that when it had innumerable sins to answer for, it received not punishment, but obtained pardon, and infinite favors. For if one, whose servant had committed many offenses, instead of scourging him with thongs, should grant him a pardon for all those, but should require an account of his future conduct, and bid him beware of falling into the same faults again, and should bestow high favors upon him, who do you think would not be overcome at hearing of such kindness? But do not think that grace stops at the pardon of former sins-it secures us against them in future, for this also is of grace. Since if He were never to punish those who still do amiss, this would not be so much grace, as encouragement to evil and wickedness.

"For the grace of God," he says, "hath appeared, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present world; looking for the blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ." See, how together with the rewards he places the virtue. And this is of grace, to deliver us from worldly things, and to lead us to Heaven. He speaks here of two appearings; for there are two; the first of grace, the second of retribution and justice.

"That denying ungodliness," he says, "and worldly lusts."

See here the foundation of all virtue. He has not said "avoiding," but "denying." Denying implies the greatest distance, the greatest hatred and aversion. With as much resolution and zeal as they turned from idols, with so much let them turn from vice itself, and worldly lusts. For these too are idols, that is, worldly lusts, and covetousness, and this he names idolatry. Whatever things are useful for the present life are worldly lusts, whatever things perish with the present life are worldly lusts. Let us then have nothing to do with these. Christ came, "that we should deny ungodliness." Ungodliness relates to doctrines, worldly lusts to a wicked life.

"And should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present world."

Dost thou see, what I always affirm, that it is not sobriety only to abstain from fornication, but that we must be free from other passions. So then he who loves wealth is not sober. For as the fornicator loves women, so the other loves money, and even more inordinately, for he is not impelled by so strong a passion. And he is certainly a more powerless charioteer who cannot manage a gentle horse, than he who cannot restrain a wild and unruly one.
Commentary on Titus

For the grace of God the Savior has shone forth to all men, instructing us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live chastely, and justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a choice people, an emulator of good works. After the catalogue of doctrine to Titus, of what he ought to instruct the old men, what the old women, what the young women and the young men, what, lastly, the slaves, he now rightly adds: For the grace of God the Savior has shone forth to all men. For there is no difference at all between free and slave, Greek and barbarian, the circumcised and the one who has a foreskin, woman and man: but we are all one in Christ, we are all called to the kingdom of God, all of us after the offense are to be reconciled to our Father; not through our merits, but through the grace of the Savior: either because Christ himself is the living and subsisting grace of God the Father, or because this is the grace of Christ, God the Savior; and we have been saved not by our own merit, according to what is said in another place: "For nothing you will save them" (Ps. 55:8).
SERMONS 23.5

Wherefore since the loving-kindness is manifest, dearly beloved, wherewith all the riches of Divine goodness are showered on us, whose call to eternal life has been assisted not only by the profitable examples of those who went before, but also by the visible and bodily appearing of the Truth Itself, we are bound to keep the day of the Lord's Nativity with no slothful nor carnal joy. And we shall each keep it worthily and thoroughly, if we remember of what Body we are members, and to what a Head we are joined, lest any one as an ill-fitting joint cohere not with the rest of the sacred building.
The Divine Institutes Book 5, Chapter XXIV

Whatever, therefore, wicked princes plan against us, God Himself permits to be done. And yet most unjust persecutors, to whom the name of God was a subject of reproach and mockery, must not think that they will escape with impunity, because they have been, as it were, the ministers of His indignation against us. For they will be punished with the judgment of God, who, having received power, have abused it to an inhuman degree, and have even insulted God in their arrogance, and placed His eternal name beneath their feet, to be impiously and wickedly trampled upon. On this account He promises that He will quickly take vengeance upon them, and exterminate the evil monsters from the earth. But He also, although He is accustomed to avenge the persecutions of His people even in the present world, commands us, however, to await patiently that day of heavenly judgment, in which He Himself will honour or punish every man according to his deserts. Therefore let not the souls of the sacrilegious expect that those whom they thus trample upon will be despised and unavenged. Those ravenous and voracious wolves who have tormented just and innocent souls, without the commission of any crimes, will surely meet with their reward. Only let us labour, that nothing else in us may be punished by men but righteousness alone: let us strive with all our power that we may at once deserve at the hands of God the avenging of our suffering and a reward.
Commentary on Titus

This grace has shone forth to all men for this reason: to instruct us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live chastely and justly and piously in this age. And what it is to deny impiety and worldly desires, I trust can be understood from what we expounded above, "They confess that they know God, but in deeds they deny him", opposites being explained through their opposites. Worldly desires, then, are those which are suggested by the prince of this world: and since they belong to the age, they pass away with the cloud of this age. But when we have lived chastely and justly in Christ, sinning, that is, neither in body nor in mind, we shall also live piously in this age: and this piety awaits the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ.
TRACTATES ON JOHN 17.4

Now fasting, in its large and general sense, is to abstain from the iniquities and unlawful pleasures of the world, which is perfect fasting: "That, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we may live temperately, and righteously, and godly in this present world." What reward does the apostle join to this fast? He goes on to say: "Looking for that blessed hope, and the appearing of the glory of the blessed God, and our Saviour Jesus Christ." In this world, then, we celebrate, as it were, the forty days' abstinence, when we live aright, and abstain from iniquities and from unlawful pleasures. But because this abstinence shall not be without reward, we look for "that blessed hope, and the revelation of the glory of the great God, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ." In that hope, when the reality of the hope shall have come to pass, we shall receive our wages, a penny.
SERMONS 223.2

Paul must receive, embrace and observe, without any reserve, those commandments of the law which help to form the character of the faithful, such as that "denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly and justly and godly in this world" and "Thou shalt not covet," chosen by the apostle as the part of the law worthy of the greatest commendation; and also the commandments about loving God and our neighbor, as set forth in the law without any figure or mystery.… But whatever progress he makes in them he must not attribute it to himself but to "the grace of God by Jesus Christ our Lord." Letters 196.2.8.Fulgentius of Ruspe: The apostle Paul exclaims in a similar way: "Be imitators of God as his dear children." What will we reply to these words, brethren, or what excuse will we be able to have? If someone tells you that you should imitate the powers which our Lord exercised, there is a reasonable excuse for you, because not everyone is given the grace to exercise those powers and to work miracles. Often considering with myself what the word περιούσιον might mean, and asking the wise men of this age whether they had perhaps read it anywhere, I could never find anyone to explain to me what it signified. Therefore I was compelled to have recourse to the old instrument, from which I supposed the Apostle too had taken what he had said. For a Hebrew of the Hebrews, and as to the law a Pharisee, he was surely setting down in his Epistle what he knew he had read in the Old Testament. So in Deuteronomy I found: "For you are a holy people to the Lord your God, and it has pleased the Lord your God in you that you should be to him a people περιούσιον out of all the peoples that are upon the face of the earth" (Deut. 7:6). And in the hundred and thirty-fourth Psalm, where we have, "Sing psalms to his name, for it is sweet: for the Lord has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel for a possession (in possessione) for himself" (Ps. 134:3–4): for what is "for a possession" (in possessione), in the Greek it is written εἰς περιουσιασμὸν, which Aquila and the Fifth Edition indeed expressed as εἰς περιούσιον. But the Seventy and Theodotion, translating περιουσιασμὸν, made a change of syllable, not of sense. Symmachus, then, for what is περιούσιον in the Greek, SGOLLA (סגלה) in the Hebrew, expressed ἐξαίρετον, that is, "choice" (egregium), or "special" (præcipuum); for which word, using the Latin language in another volume, he rendered "peculiar" (peculiarem). Rightly, then, did Christ Jesus, our great God and Savior, redeem us with his blood, to make the Christian people peculiar to himself, a people that could then be peculiar if it proved an emulator of good works. Hence also what is written in the Gospel according to the Latin translators, "Give us this day our daily (quotidianum) bread" (Matt. 6:11), is better rendered in the Greek "our bread ἐπιούσιον", that is, "special", "choice", "peculiar": namely him who, coming down from heaven, says, "I am the bread that came down from heaven" (John 6:51). Far be it, indeed, that we, who are forbidden to take thought for the morrow, should be commanded in the Lord's prayer to ask for that bread which in a little while is to be digested and cast out into the drain. Nor is there much difference between ἐπιούσιον and περιούσιον: for only the preposition has been changed, not the word. Some think that the bread in the Lord's prayer is called ἐπιούσιον because it is above all οὐσίας, that is, above all substances. If this is accepted, it does not differ much from the sense we have set out. For whatever is choice and special is outside all things and above all things.

Ver. 15. "These things speak and exhort, and rebuke with all authority."
