Speak these things and exhort, and rebuke with all authority. He has set down three things: speak, exhort, and rebuke. And what he says, speak, seems to refer to doctrine. But what he has added, exhort (exhortare), that is, παρακάλει, means something different in the Greek from what it means in the Latin: for παράκλησις means comfort rather than exhortation. He used this word above too about the young men: "Comfort (consolare) the young men likewise to be chaste in all things". In its own place we rendered it as it is read in the Latin, as though "exhort" were written. He, then, comforts his hearer who says, "We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20), and humbles and subjects himself, to gain the one he comforts. But the third thing, rebuke, seems to me to be the opposite of comfort, so that whoever has despised comfort is worthy of rebuke, and deserves to hear: "You have forgotten the comfort which speaks to you as to sons". To Timothy also we read of comfort as one thing and rebuke as another, as the Apostle says: "Be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, comfort" (2 Tim. 4:2). And there, indeed, rebuke is taken up first, and afterward severity is tempered by comfort. Here, however, he wants the disciples first to be comforted, and, if they have not profited by the comforting, then to be reproved, and reproved with all authority. For so I understand what has been said, rebuke with all authority: that it refers specifically to rebuke, and not to the two preceding in common. For it is not fitting to say, comfort with all authority, and speak with all authority, but only, rebuke with all authority.

Let no one despise you. Someone might think that this is the very same thing now written to Titus that was said to Timothy: "Let no one despise your youth" (1 Tim. 4:12). But we, following the distinction of the Greek language, think that περιφρονείτω, which is written here, means one thing, and καταφρονείτω, which was said to Timothy, another, and that the prepositions περὶ and κατὰ make a different sense. And that the apostle Paul uses, not by chance and at whim, different nouns and verbs, and even different prepositions, according to the variety of the matters, can be made plain from what he says: "For the woman is from the man, but the man through the woman" (1 Cor. 11:12). And elsewhere: "For from him and through him and in him are all things" (Rom. 11:36). And also this: "Paul an apostle, not from men, nor through man" (Gal. 1:1). We think, therefore, that καταφρόνησιν properly pertains to contempt, as when someone, stretched on the rack and among the hot plates, despises pain, and fears neither the threats of the judge nor the roar of the crowd standing around, but for the confession of martyrdom despises and disdains all torments. On the other hand there is also an evil contempt, of which Habakkuk too, the Holy Spirit speaking in him, testifies: "Behold, you despisers, and look, and wonder at wonders, and perish" (Hab. 1:5). According to which we have said that it was written to Timothy also: "Let no one despise your youth" (1 Tim. 4:12), that is: I do not want you to show yourself such that you could deservedly be despised by anyone. Περιφρόνησις, however, means this, as the Stoics at any rate assert, who distinguish subtly between words: when someone, trusting in himself that he is better than another, looks down on the one he thinks inferior, and, being above, that is, wiser, judges the humbler man worthy of contempt. Something of this kind a certain person among the Greeks, swelling with the vanity of pride and looking down on heaven itself and the sun, is mocked for having said: Ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον, which we can say in Latin: I climb through the air, and I know myself to be worth more than the sun. Περιφρόνησις, then, which is now set down to Titus, has this sense: Let no one of those who are in the churches, while you act sluggishly, so live as to think himself the better. For what sort of edification will there be for the disciple if he perceives that he is greater than his master? Hence not only bishops, presbyters and deacons ought to take great care to go before all the people over whom they preside in conduct and in speech, but also the lower rank: exorcists, readers, sacristans, and absolutely all who serve the house of God. For it greatly destroys the Church of Christ that laymen should be better than clerics.

n: Princes and powers. At the time St. Paul wrote this epistle to Titus, there were many Jews, particularly the disciples of Judas of Gaulan, who maintained that the Hebrews were under no obligation of obeying any other than God, or at most the rulers of their own nation. A man that is, &c. Many ancient copies have this passage thus, Avoid a heretic after one reprehension. (Rom. xiv. 10.) But if they are not true, how great the fire. Hear what the thief says to his fellow-thief. "For we are also in the same condemnation." (Luke xxiii. 40.) Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey; to be ready for every good work; to blaspheme no one, not to be quarrelsome; to be modest, showing all gentleness toward all men. Something of the kind is written to the Romans as well: "Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God" (Rom. 13:1). This precept, both here and there, I think was issued for this reason: that at that time the doctrine of Judas the Galilean was still flourishing and had very many followers. Mention of him is made also in the Acts of the Apostles, where Scripture relates: "For before these days Theudas rose up, saying that he was someone great; and about three thousand men joined him" (Acts 5:36); and, "after him rose up Judas the Galilean in the days of the census". Among other things he put forward this as if it were plausible from the Law: that no one ought to be called Lord except God alone, and that those who brought tithes to the temple should not pay tribute to Caesar. This heresy had grown so much that it troubled a great part even of the Pharisees and of the people, so that this question was brought even to our Lord: "Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not" (Matt. 22:17)? Answering them prudently and cautiously, the Lord says: "Render the things that are Caesar's to Caesar, and the things that are God's to God" (ibid. 21). In agreement with this answer, the apostle Paul teaches that believers ought to be subject to principalities and authorities. For Ἀρχαὶ, which is read in the Greek, sounds more like "principalities" (principatus) than "rulers" (principes), and signifies the authority itself, not the men who are in authority. But because he had said, "Remind them to be subject to principalities and authorities", an occasion for denial could be given to those who dread torments: they might claim, according to the Apostle's saying, that they were subject to principalities and authorities and were doing what these commanded; therefore he added: To obey for every good work. If what the emperor and the governor command is good, comply with the will of the one who commands. But if it is evil and savors of what is against God, answer him with that saying from the Acts of the apostles: "One must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). Let us understand this same thing of servants toward their masters, of wives toward their husbands, and of children toward their parents: that they ought to be subject to masters, husbands and parents only in those things that do not go against the commandments of God. What follows, To be ready, is to be read in two ways: either so that "to be ready for every good work" is understood; or else, joining what he says, to obey for every good work, with what precedes and ending it there, to be ready is, as it were, another precept of its own and a special one, in keeping with what is written in Leviticus: "The goat that is sent away, bearing the curses of the people, is to be handed over into the hands of a ready man" (Lev. 16:21). If, then, anyone is ready to hold the ἀποπομπαῖον (the scapegoat), and lead it out into the desert, and there destroy it, and, so far as in him lies, banish it by the lot of the curse, he, when he has obeyed, will also be ready for every good work. To be ready can also be taken in another way: that they should picture to themselves beforehand in their minds everything that can happen, so that when it does happen they suffer nothing as if it were new, but all things have been prepared for them in advance.
Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews.

No one, too, to blaspheme, is not taken simply. For he does not say, to blaspheme no man, but absolutely, no one: not an angel, not any creature of God. For all things that were made by God are very good. "When Michael the archangel was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy, but said, May God command you" (Jude 9). If, then, Michael did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy against the devil, who was surely most deserving of a curse, how much more ought we to be pure of every curse? The devil deserved a curse; but blasphemy ought not to come out through the archangel's mouth. Read the old books again, and see which tribes were stationed on Mount Gerizim to bless the people, and which on the other mount to curse. Reuben, who had defiled his father's bed, and Zebulun, the last son of Leah, and the children of the handmaids are placed on Mount Ebal to curse those who are worthy of cursing (Deut. 27). It would take long if I were now to recount how Jacob, who had called his sons to a blessing (Gen. 49:1), saying, "that I may bless you", afterward joins, as if within the blessing, "cursed be their fury, because it was headstrong"; and how the Lord himself speaks in Genesis: "Cursed is the ground in your works" (Gen. 3:17). Let it suffice now to have said only this: that the disciples of Christ ought not to blaspheme, nor, as is added, to be quarrelsome. For if we are sons of peace, and wish peace to rest upon us, and have come to the heavenly Jerusalem, which took its name from peace, let us have peace with those who hate peace, and, so far as in us lies, let us be peaceable with all men: not only with the modest but also with brawlers, since there is no virtue in bearing with the gentle; and let us give place to wrath, showing all gentleness toward all men: not that we ought, from a desire for vainglory, to show ourselves gentle to all men, but that, while we bear with all and do not repay injury in kind, our very works may become better known to all. Someone can, for the sake of boasting and the opinion of the crowd and popular favor, feign gentleness before certain people and pretend goodness. But where there is no true, genuine and solid gentleness, I do not know whether all can be persuaded that he is gentle.

Ver. 3. "For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish."

Thus also he does in his Epistle to the Galatians, where he says, "Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world." (Gal. iv. 4.) Therefore he says, Revile no one, for such also thou wast thyself.

"For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another."

Therefore we ought to be thus to all, to be gently disposed. But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and fights that come from the Law: for they are useless and vain. Because questions are manifold and diverse, Solomon therefore spoke about those who seek God, saying: "But those who seek him rightly have found peace" (Prov. 16:8). Those, then, who do not seek God rightly cannot find peace. There are very many examples of those who seek God not rightly. The Jews seek God perversely, hoping that they can find him without Christ. The heretics, clattering with an empty din of words, seek one whom they cannot find. Philosophers too, and barbarians, holding various views about God, have sought God. But because they did not seek rightly, their questions were foolish, since they thought that God could be comprehended by human senses. From these questions, then, Paul calls us back. But to wise questions, and to those propped up by the authority of the Scriptures, he rather exhorts and summons us, not unaware of the precepts of the Savior, in which he says: "Seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened to you, ask and it will be given to you. For everyone who seeks finds, and who asks receives, and to him who knocks it will be opened" (Luke 11); only let our body not be subject to sins, and wisdom will enter into us. Let the understanding be exercised, let the mind be fed daily with divine reading, and our questions will not be foolish questions. And what he says, "Avoid genealogies and contentions and quarrels that come from the Law", strikes properly at the Jews, who boast in this and think they have knowledge of the Law if they hold the names of individuals: names which, because they are barbarous and we do not know their etymologies, are generally pronounced corruptly by us. And if perhaps we have erred in accent, in the length and shortness of a syllable, either lengthening short ones or shortening long ones, they are wont to laugh at us for our lack of skill, especially in the aspirates and in pronouncing certain letters with a scraping of the throat. This has come about because the Seventy translators, through whom the divine Law was translated into the Greek tongue, expressed in particular the letter HETH, and AIN, and others of this kind (because they could not carry them over into the Greek language with a double aspiration), by adding other letters. For example, so that for Rahel they said Rachel, and for Jeriho, Jericho, and for Hebron, Chebron, and for Seor, Segor; but in other cases this attempt fails them. For we and the Greeks have only one letter s, but they have three, SAMECH, SADE and SIN, which have different sounds. Isaac and Sion are written with SADE; Israel with SIN, and yet it does not sound as it is written. Seon, king of the Amorites, is both pronounced and written with the letter SAMECH. If, then, these idioms of the names and of the language, being of course barbarous, have not been expressed by us as they are expressed by the Hebrews, they are wont to raise a guffaw and to swear that they have no idea at all what we are saying. Hence it has also been our care to correct, from the originals themselves, all the books of the old Law which the learned man Adamantius had arranged in the Hexapla, copied from the library of Caesarea; in these both the Hebrew words themselves are written out in their own characters and they are expressed in Greek letters in the adjoining column. Aquila also and Symmachus, the Seventy too and Theodotion keep their own order. Some books, however, and especially those which among the Hebrews are composed in verse, have three other editions added, which they call the fifth, sixth and seventh translation, editions that have gained authority without the names of their translators. That immortal genius bestowed these things on us by his own labor, so that we need not greatly fear the haughtiness of the Jews, who delight in loosened lips, a twisted tongue, hissing saliva and a scraped throat. They have also another occasion for pride: just as we who are Latins more easily commit to memory Latin names having their origins from our own tongue, so they from an early age, with their innermost senses, have drunk in the native words of their speech, and from the beginning, Adam, to the last, Zerubbabel, they run through the generations of all so readily and swiftly from memory that you would think they were reciting their own name. We, who either learned other letters, or certainly believed in Christ late, or, even if we were given over to the Church as infants, pursue the sense of the Scriptures rather than the words: if perhaps we do not know this so well, they think themselves more learned in reciting names, in reckoning years, and in grandsons and great-great-grandsons, grandfathers, great-grandfathers and great-great-great-grandfathers. But since, like their leader, they too go about like lions seeking whom among the simple they shall devour, we are compelled to write in reply to your piety, that the brethren being once again instructed by your admonition may still further reprove the vain teaching of those men.
LETTERS 22

He who has been corrected in first faults, and received pardon, if he sins again prepares for himself a judgment of wrath worse than the former. He, who after the first and second admonition abides in his fault, ought to be brought before the person in authority, if haply after being rebuked by more he may be ashamed. If even thus he fail to be set right he is to be cut off from the rest as one that maketh to offend, and regarded as a heathen and a publican, for the security of them that are obedient, according to the saying, When the impious fall the righteous tremble.
Exposition of the Christian Faith 1.6.47

This monster's cavern [of heresies], your sacred Majesty, is thick laid (as seafaring men do say it is) with hidden lairs, and all the surrounding neighborhood, where the rocks of unbelief echo to the howling of her black dogs, we must pass by with ears stopped up. For it is written: "Hedge your ears about with thorns" and again: "Beware of dogs. Beware of evil workers"; and yet again: "One who is a heretic, avoid after the first reproof knowing that such a one is fallen and is in sin, being condemned of his own judgment." So then, like prudent pilots, let us set the sails of our faith for the course wherein we may pass by most safely and again follow the coasts of the Scriptures.
Homily on Titus 6

How then does he elsewhere say, "If God peradventure will give them repentance" (2 Tim. ii. 25); but here, "A man that is an heretic after the first and second admonition reject, knowing that he that is such is subverted and sinneth, being condemned of himself"? In the former passage he speaks of the correction of those of whom he had hope, and who had simply made opposition. But when he is known and manifest to all, why dost thou contend in vain? why dost thou beat the air? What means, "being condemned of himself"? Because he cannot say that no one has told him, no one admonished him; since therefore after admonition he continues the same, he is self-condemned.

What then? dost thou command him to stop the mouths of gainsayers, if he must pass them by when they are doing everything to their own destruction? He means that he should not do it principally for their advantage, for being once perverted in their minds, they would not profit by it. But if they injured others, it behooved him to withstand and contend with them; and manfully await them, but if thou art reduced to necessity, seeing them destroying others, be not silent, but stop their mouths, from regard to those whom they would destroy. It is not indeed possible for a zealous man of upright life to abstain from contention, but so do as I have said. For the evil arises from idleness and a vain philosophy, that one should be occupied about words only. For it is a great injury to be uttering a superfluity of words, when one ought to be teaching, or praying, or giving thanks. For it is not right to be sparing of our money but not sparing of our words; we ought rather to spare words than our money, and not to give ourselves up to all sorts of persons.

What means, "that they be careful to maintain good works"? That they wait not for those who are in want to come to them, but that they seek out those who need their assistance. Thus the considerate man shows his concern, and with great zeal will he perform this duty. For in doing good actions, it is not those who receive the kindness that are benefited, so much as those who do it that make gain and profit, for it gives them confidence towards God. But in the other case, there is no end of contention: therefore he calls the heretic incorrigible. For as to neglect those for whom there is a hope of conversion is the part of slothfulness, so to bestow pains upon those who are diseased past remedy is the extreme of folly and madness; for we render them more bold.
Commentary on Titus

Avoid a heretical man after one and a second reproof, knowing that such a one is subverted, and sins, being condemned by himself. The name of heresy is used also in the Epistle to the Corinthians: "For there must also be heresies among us, so that those who are approved may become manifest" (1 Cor. 11:19). And to the Galatians it is numbered among the works of the flesh: "Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, contentions, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envyings, drunkennesses, revellings, and other things like these, which I foretell to you as I have foretold: that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God" (Gal. 5:19 ff.). In these it must be carefully observed that, just as the other vices which are numbered among the works of the flesh exclude us from the kingdom of God, so heresies too take the kingdom of God away from us; and it makes no difference in what way anyone is excluded from the kingdom, so long as he is excluded. And, what may be more wonderful, that passage from the Acts of the apostles also seems worth reading again, where our faith in Christ and the discipline of the Church were already then called a heresy by perverse men. "For we", say the Jews to the apostle Paul, "have neither received letters from you from Judea, nor has any of the brethren come and reported to us, or anyone spoken evil of you. But we ask to hear from you what you think; for concerning this heresy it is known to us that it is everywhere spoken against" (Acts 28:21, 22). And although the name of heresy is not spoken at Miletus, yet its works are named by Paul when he speaks to the presbyters of the church: "I know that after my departure grievous wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among yourselves men will rise up speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them" (Acts 20:29, 30). Let these things be said in passing, about where else too heresy is so named. Now the name itself seems to need to be sifted most fully. Heresy is named in Greek "from choice" (electio), because each one chooses for himself what seems to him better. The philosophers too, Stoics, Peripatetics, Academics, Epicureans, are said to be of this or that heresy. It is superfluous to go through them one by one and to enumerate Marcion, Valentinus, Apelles, Ebion, Montanus and Manichaeus with their doctrines, since it is very easy for anyone to know by what errors each is led. Arius and Eunomius, and the author of a new heresy: would that they were not so well known; perhaps they would have deceived fewer! Avoid, then, a heretical man after one reproof, or, as the Greek has it better, νουθεσίαν; and νουθεσία signifies rather admonition and teaching without rebuke. In the Latin manuscripts is read (and Pope Athanasius too approved it as true): "After one and a second reproof"; namely that it is not enough for one who is depraved by some error to be reproved or admonished only once, but a second teaching too must be applied to him, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand.
ON PRESCRIPTION AGAINST HERETICS 6

It is the same Paul who, in his epistle to the Galatians, counts "heresies" among "the sins of the flesh," who also intimates to Titus that "a man who is a heretic" must be "rejected after the first admonition." This is on the ground that "he that is perverted and commits sin as a self-condemned man." Indeed, in almost every epistle, when enjoining on us [the duty] of avoiding false doctrines, he sharply condemns heresies. Of these the practical effects are false doctrines, called in Greek heresis, a word used in the sense of that choice which a man makes when he either teaches them [to others] or takes up with them [for himself]. For this reason it is that he calls the heretic self-condemned, because he has himself chosen that in which he is condemned.
Epistle LXXIII

He forbade one coming from any heresy to be baptized in the Church; that is, he judged the baptism of all heretics to be just and lawful. And although special heresies have special baptisms and different sins, he, holding communion with the baptism of all, gathered up the sins of all, heaped together into his own bosom. And he charged that nothing should be innovated except what had been handed down; as if he were an innovator, who, holding the unity, claims for the one Church one baptism; and not manifestly he who, forgetful of unity, adopts the lies and the contagions of a profane washing. Let nothing be innovated, says he, nothing maintained, except what has been handed down. Whence is that tradition? Whether does it descend from the authority of the Lord and of the Gospel, or does it come from the commands and the epistles of the apostles? For that those things which are written must be done, God witnesses and admonishes, saying to Joshua the son of Nun: "The book of this law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate in it day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein." Also the Lord, sending His apostles, commands that the nations should be baptized, and taught to observe all things which He commanded. If, therefore, it is either prescribed in the Gospel, or contained in the epistles or Acts of the Apostles, that those who come from any heresy should not be baptized, but only hands laid upon them to repentance, let this divine and holy tradition be observed. But if everywhere heretics are called nothing else than adversaries and antichrists, if they are pronounced to be people to be avoided, and to be perverted and condemned of their own selves, wherefore is it that they should not be thought worthy of being condemned by us, since it is evident from the apostolic testimony that they are of their own selves condemned? So that no one ought to defame the apostles as if they had approved of the baptisms of heretics, or had communicated with them without the Church's baptism, when they, the apostles, wrote such things of the heretics. And this, too, while as yet the more terrible plagues of heresy had not broken forth; while Marcion of Pontus had not yet emerged from Pontus, whose master Cerdon came to Rome,-while Hyginus was still bishop, who was the ninth bishop in that city,-whom Marcion followed, and with greater impudence adding other enhancements to his crime, and more daringly set himself to blaspheme against God the Father, the Creator, and armed with sacrilegious arms the heretical madness that rebelled against the Church with greater wickedness and determination.
Epistle LXXV.4

For the faith of the sacred Scripture sets forth that the Church is not without, nor can be separated nor divided against itself, but maintains the unity of an inseparable and undivided house; since it is written of the sacrament of the passover, and of the lamb, which Lamb designated Christ: "In one house shall it be eaten: ye shall not carry forth the flesh abroad out of the house." Which also we see expressed concerning Rahab, who herself also bore a type of the Church, who received the command which said, "Thou shalt bring thy father, and thy mother, and thy brethren, and all thy father's household unto thee into thine house; and whosoever shall go out of the doors of thine house into the street, his blood shall be upon him." In which mystery is declared, that they who will live, and escape from the destruction of the world, must be gathered together into one house alone, that is, into the Church; but whosoever of those thus collected together shall go out abroad, that is, if any one, although he may have obtained grace in the Church, shall depart and go out of the Church, that his blood shall be upon him; that is, that he himself must charge it upon himself that he perishes; which the Apostle Paul explains, teaching and enjoining that a heretic must be avoided, as perverse, and a sinner, and as condemned of himself. For that man will be guilty of his own ruin, who, not being cast out by the bishop, but of his own accord deserting from the Church is by heretical presumption condemned of himself.
Commentary on Titus

And why he is to be avoided after a first and second reproof, he gives the reasons, saying: "that such a one is subverted, and sins, since he is condemned by himself". For he who, reproved once and twice, having heard his error, does not wish to be corrected, thinks the one correcting him is in error; and on the contrary, preparing himself for fights and wranglings of words, he wants to win over the one by whom he is taught. He is said to be condemned by himself for this reason: because the fornicator, the adulterer, the murderer and the other vices are driven out of the Church through the priests; but heretics pass sentence on themselves, withdrawing from the Church by their own choice; and this withdrawal seems to be a condemnation by their own conscience. Between heresy and schism they think the difference is this: that heresy holds a perverse doctrine, while schism separates from the Church on account of episcopal dissension; which indeed can be understood in some measure at the beginning. But there is no schism that does not invent some heresy for itself, so that it may seem to have withdrawn from the Church rightly.
Homily on Titus 6

Ver. 12. "When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus; be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis." What sayest thou? After having appointed him to preside over Crete, dost thou again summon him to thyself? It was not to withdraw him from that occupation, but to discipline him the more for it. For that he does not call him to attend upon him, as if he took him everywhere with him as his follower, appears from what he adds:

"For I have determined there to winter."

Now Nicopolis is a city of Thrace.
Commentary on Titus

When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis; for there I have decided to winter. We read at the beginning of this Epistle: "For this reason I left you in Crete, that you may correct the things that were lacking, and appoint presbyters in the cities, as I arranged for you". This was so that, since the Cretans had recently believed, they should not be left orphans when Paul withdrew and passed on to other churches, but should have an apostolic man to correct the things that seemed to be lacking. Since, then, after the foundation of other churches Titus was needed to build the structure upon it, he writes to him that when he had sent Artemas or Tychicus, that is, one of the two who had been with him, to Crete, to fill his place, he himself should come to Nicopolis, declaring that he would winter there. From this we prove Paul's fatherly affection toward the Cretans. He needs Titus for the ministry of the Gospel; yet he does not want him to come to him before Artemas or Tychicus has arrived as successor in his place. Nicopolis is the city which received its name from the victory of Augustus, because there he overcame Antony and Cleopatra.
Homily on Titus 6

Ver. 14. "Bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them."

These were not of the number to whom Churches had been intrusted, but of the number of his companions. But Apollos was the more vehement, being "an eloquent man, and mighty in the Scriptures." (Acts xviii. 24.) But if Zenas was a lawyer, you say, he ought not to have been supported by others. But by a lawyer here is meant one versed in the laws of the Jews. And he seems to say, supply their wants abundantly, that nothing may be lacking to them.
Commentary on Titus

Send Zenas, the teacher of the law, and Apollos ahead with care, so that nothing may be lacking to them. This is the Apollos about whom it is written to the Corinthians too: "Each of you says: I am of Paul, but I of Apollos, and I of Cephas" (1 Cor. 1:12). He was a man of Alexandria, of the Jews, very eloquent and perfect in the Law, bishop of the Corinthians. Because of the dissensions that were at Corinth, it is to be supposed that he crossed over with Zenas, the teacher of the law, to the neighboring island of Crete, and that, when the dissensions that had arisen at Corinth were calmed by Paul's Epistle, he returned again to Corinth. As for Zenas, the teacher of the law, we cannot say from any other place of Scripture who he was, except only this: that he too, an apostolic man, had the same work that Apollos was doing, that of building up the churches of Christ. He therefore instructs Titus that, since they were about to sail from Crete to Greece, he should not let them be in need of provisions, but should see that they have what is necessary for provisions for the journey.
On the Work of Monks 15.16

Nevertheless, after the apostle had said in such instruction and advice: "Now such persons we charge and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that they work quietly and eat their own bread," he was mindful of such needs of the holy persons who, although they would obey his commands to work quietly and eat their own bread, would, for many reasons, lack some provision of such necessary commodities. Hence, with foresight he added immediately: "But you, brothers, do not grow tired of well-doing," so that those who had the means of furnishing sustenance to the servants of God would not grow careless in this respect. Furthermore, when in writing to Titus he said: "Help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, taking care that nothing be wanting to them." He continued thus, in order to show why nothing should be lacking in their regard: "And let the people also learn to excel in good works, in order to meet cases of necessity, that they may not be unfruitful."
Homily on Titus 6

Ver. 14, 15. "And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful. All that are with me salute thee. Greet them that love us in the faith."

That is, either those that love Paul himself, or those men that are faithful.

"Grace be with you all. Amen."

"And let ours," he says, "learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful." You observe that he is more anxious for them than for those who are to receive their kindnesses. For they might probably have been brought on their way by many others, but I am concerned, he says, for our own friends. For what advantage would it be to them, if others should dig up treasures, and maintain their teachers? This would be no benefit to them, for they remained unfruitful. Could not Christ then, Who with five loaves fed five thousand men, and with seven loaves fed four thousand, could not He have supported Himself and His disciples?

For what reason then was He maintained by women? For women, it is said, followed Him, and ministered unto Him. (Mark xv. 41.) It was to teach us from the first that He is concerned for those who do good. Could not Paul, who supported others by his own hands, have maintained himself without assistance from others? But you see him receiving and requesting aid. And hear the reason for it. "Not because I desire a gift," he says, "but I desire fruit that may abound to your account." (Phil. iv. 17.)
Commentary on Titus

But let ours also learn to be foremost in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful. Above he had said: "Send Zenas, the teacher of the Law, and Apollos ahead with care, so that nothing may be lacking to them". Since, then, a hidden reply could arise, so that not so much Titus as any reader of the Epistle might say this: "And from what means is Titus to bestow on them, since they have no provisions for the journey?", he resolves this question and, as if no objection were put to him, strikes it down by saying: But let ours also learn to be foremost in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful. He calls his own "ours", those who had believed in Christ: because they were Christ's, they rightly deserved to be called both Paul's and Titus's. You have, he says, authority over the disciples; teach them not to be unfruitful, but to minister to the evangelists and apostolic men who serve good works; and to minister not in any matters whatever, but for necessary uses: "For having food and clothing, let us be content with these" (1 Tim. 6:8); and let those who serve the altar live from the altar; and those who have become partakers of our spiritual things ought to share their carnal things with us. And lest perhaps they should easily despise either Paul's letter or Titus's precept, he calls unfruitful all who have not ministered to the evangelists. Solomon too says in Proverbs: "But almsgiving is fruit" (Prov. 3:9). And Paul himself calls love the first fruit of the spirit (Gal. 5). Love, however, is proved above all in sharing and in ministry. So that they may not, he says, be unfruitful. "For every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire" (Matt. 3:10). Now I say this because he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. To be unwilling to give to apostolic men and to the evangelizers of Christ for necessary uses is to condemn oneself of barrenness.
Commentary on Titus

All who are with me greet you. Either he used the customary formula, saying that Titus was greeted by all who were with him; or else he says it properly of Titus, because he was such as to deserve the love of all who were with Paul. And it is great praise of Titus to be greeted through Paul by all.

Greet those who love us in faith. If everyone who loves loved in faith, and there were not others who love without faith, Paul would never have added faith to love, saying: Greet those who love us in faith. For mothers too love their sons, so much that they are ready to meet death for them; but they do not love in faith. And wives love their husbands, with whom they very often die; but that love is not of faith. Only the love of the saints loves in faith, so much so that, even if the one who is loved is an unbeliever, the saint nevertheless loves him in faith, according to that saying: "Let all your things be done in faith" (1 Cor. 16:14). And elsewhere: "Love your enemies" (Luke 6:35). The saint loves his enemies, and therefore loves in faith, because he believes in him who promised that he would render a reward for the fulfilling of the commandment.

The grace of our Lord be with you all. It should be known that in the Greek manuscripts it is written thus: "Grace be with you all", so that neither "of the Lord" nor "our" is found in the authentic books. So he invokes grace in common upon the saints and believers, upon Titus and the others who were with him. And just as the patriarch Isaac blessed his son Jacob (Gen. 27), and he himself the twelve Patriarchs (ibid. 49), the apostles too, entering a house, used to say: "Peace to this house" (Matt. 10:12). And if the house was worthy, their peace rested upon it; but if it showed itself unworthy, it returned to those who had invoked it. So now too, at the end of his Epistle, the Apostle invokes grace upon believers: a grace which had its effect together with the prayer, and lay in the power of the believers, if the one blessed was willing to show himself such as the one who blessed him.

He had made this his beloved son Titus, chief bishop of Crete; in which island were formerly a hundred cities, on which account it was called Hecatompolis. It is now called Candy. We have a commentary of St. Jerome on this epistle, tom. iv, p. 409. E. B. (Witham) --- Titus was an uncircumcised Gentile: we know not on what occasion he attached himself to St. Paul. It is however certain that he was a great utility to St. Paul in the government of the Church. --- St. Paul having preached the faith in the island of Crete, left his beloved Titus there to finish the work which he had begun. Afterwards the apostle, on a journey to Nicopolis, a city of Macedonia, wrote this epistle to Titus; in which he directs him to ordain bishops and priests for the different cities, shewing him the principal qualities necessary for a bishop, also gives him particular advice for his own conduct to his flock, exhorting him to hold to strictness of discipline, but seasoned with lenity. It was written about thirty-three years after our Lord's ascension. (Challoner)
